headline.en: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum and Ors.: The Catalyst
headline.hi: Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum and Ors.: The Catalyst

body.en: Mohd Ahmed Khan, an advocate, married Shah Bano Begum in 1932 and had five children. In 1975, after 43 years of marriage, Khan drove Shah Bano out of the matrimonial home. In April 1978, she filed a petition before the Judicial Magistrate (First Class), Indore, under Section 125 CrPC seeking Rs. 500/month in maintenance, citing Khan's professional income of Rs. 60,000/year.
body.hi: Mohd Ahmed Khan, an advocate, married Shah Bano Begum in 1932 and had five children. In 1975, after 43 years of marriage, Khan drove Shah Bano out of the matrimonial home. In April 1978, she filed a petition before the Judicial Magistrate (First Class), Indore, under Section 125 CrPC seeking Rs. 500/month in maintenance, citing Khan's professional income of Rs. 60,000/year.

body.en: While the petition was pending, Khan divorced her by irrevocable talaq on 6 November 1978 and deposited Rs. 3,000 in court as Mahr and iddat maintenance, claiming his obligations under Muslim personal law were fully discharged. In August 1979, the Magistrate ordered Rs. 25/month. In July 1980, the Madhya Pradesh High Court in revision enhanced maintenance to Rs. 179.20/month. Khan appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, arguing that Section 125 does not override personal law and that Mahr satisfies Section 127(3)(b) CrPC.

body.en: "Section 125 is truly secular in character. It does not matter whether the parties are Hindus, Muslims, Christians or Parsis. episodes.title: SECTION 125 IS SECULAR. IT DOES NOT ASK YOUR RELIGION.

blocks.text:
Section 125 CrPC is a provision of general, secular application that does not yield to personal law. A divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself is entitled to maintenance under it, even beyond the iddat period — because Mahr is not a sum "payable on divorce" within Section 127(3)(b), and because Muslim personal law, on the Court's reading, does not contemplate leaving an indigent divorced wife without support at all.
The Court also placed on record a separate observation — not part of its operative holding — regretting that Article 44 of the Constitution, the directive to secure a Uniform Civil Code, remained unimplemented, and urging the State to act on it.

flashcards.q: Does Section 125 CrPC apply to divorced Muslim women?
flashcards.a: Yes. Section 125 is a secular, religion-neutral summary remedy aimed at preventing destitution, and personal law does not restrict its statutory application.

flashcards.q: Is payment of Mahr a ground to cancel maintenance under Section 127(3)(b) CrPC?
flashcards.a: No. Mahr is consideration paid in respect of the marriage, not a sum payable 'on divorce', and therefore does not extinguish the husband's statutory maintenance liability.

flashcards.q: Why was this case referred to a 5-Judge Constitution Bench?
flashcards.a: A 2-judge bench doubted the earlier 3-judge bench rulings in Bai Tahira (1979) and Fazlunbi (1980). Under the doctrine of coordinate precedent, only a larger 5-judge bench could reconsider the question.

Application of CrPC §125; CrPC §127(3)(b); Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937; Art. 44 Constitution of India analyzed through IRAC methodology.

source.paraText: The ruling established binding precedent under Article 141 of the Constitution of India, shaping subsequent jurisprudence.

student.ratio: Section 125 CrPC is a secular provision of general application that overrides personal law. A divorced Muslim wife unable to maintain herself is entitled to maintenance beyond the iddat period, because Mahr is consideration for marriage and is not a sum payable on divorce under Section 127(3)(b) CrPC.
student.examAngle: High-yield topic for CLAT-PG, Judiciary Mains, and AIBE under Family Law and CrPC. Focus on statutory supremacy of Section 125 CrPC over personal laws, the distinction between Mahr and Section 127(3)(b) sums, coordinate bench referral rules, and the subsequent 1986 Act jurisprudence (Danial Latifi).

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: Section 125 CrPC is a secular, summary remedy applicable uniformly across all religions to protect indigent divorced wives, and payment of Mahr does not discharge liability under Section 127(3)(b).
